title: Analyse and interpret the financial statements and physical records in an agri-business to generate managerial information

lessons.title: The financial statements of an agri-business
lessons.html:
Reading the numbers

Financial statements summarise the business's performance and position. Managers who can interpret them make better decisions about enterprises, investment and financing.

The income statement

Also called the statement of profit or loss, it shows income and expenses over a period, usually a financial year.

  • Gross farm income: sales of crops and livestock, plus changes in livestock and produce inventory values, plus other farm income.
  • Variable (directly allocable) costs: seed, fertiliser, feed, remedies, fuel, casual labour.
  • Fixed (overhead) costs: permanent salaries, depreciation, insurance, rates, administration.
  • Net farm income before interest and tax, then after interest.

The balance sheet

Also called the statement of financial position, it shows on a specific date what the business owns (assets), what it owes (liabilities) and the owner's equity (assets minus liabilities).

AssetsLiabilities
Current: cash, debtors, stock of produce, feed and inputsCurrent: creditors, overdraft, short-term loans
Medium-term: machinery, vehicles, breeding livestockMedium-term: instalment sales, medium-term loans
Long-term: land, buildings, fixed improvementsLong-term: mortgage bonds, long-term loans

The cash flow statement

Shows actual cash coming in and going out: from operations, investing (buying or selling assets) and financing (loans and repayments). A profitable farm can still fail if it runs out of cash, for example when income arrives months after harvest while input costs are paid at planting.

Livestock valuation

Livestock is a major asset. Changes in herd numbers and values affect income, so value consistently, using standard values or market values as your accountant advises, and reconcile numbers with physical counts.

lessons.title: Ratio analysis and physical records
lessons.html:
Turning statements into insight

Key financial ratios

RatioFormulaWhat it shows
Current ratioCurrent assets ÷ current liabilitiesLiquidity: ability to pay short-term debts
Debt ratioTotal liabilities ÷ total assetsSolvency: share of assets financed by debt
Return on assets(Net farm income + interest paid) ÷ total assetsProfitability of all capital used
Return on equityNet income after interest ÷ owner's equityReturn on the owner's own capital
Gross margin ratioGross margin ÷ gross incomeEfficiency of enterprise production
Interest coverNet farm income before interest ÷ interestAbility to carry debt

Ratios are meaningful only when compared: with previous years, budgets, study group benchmarks or bank requirements.

Worked example

A farm has current assets of R2,4 million and current liabilities of R1,6 million. The current ratio is 2,4 ÷ 1,6 = 1,5. Total assets are R30 million and total liabilities R9 million, so the debt ratio is 9 ÷ 30 = 0,30, or 30%. Equity is R21 million.

Physical records

Financial figures must be read together with physical records:

  • Crop: hectares planted, yield per hectare, quality grades, inputs per hectare, rainfall.
  • Livestock: herd numbers by class, births, deaths, sales, weaning weights, calving percentage, stocking rate.
  • Labour: hours or days by enterprise.
  • Machinery: hours, fuel use, repairs.

Physical records explain financial results. A fall in beef income may be due to fewer calves weaned (a fertility problem), lighter calves (nutrition or drought) or a lower price (market). Each points to a different management response.

lessons.title: Generating management information
lessons.html:
From analysis to decisions

Enterprise analysis

Allocate income and variable costs to each enterprise to calculate gross margins per hectare, per head or per unit of the limiting resource. Compare enterprises and identify those that carry the business and those that drain it. Remember that some enterprises support others, for example cattle using crop residues.

Cost of production

Calculate cost per unit (R per tonne, per kg of beef, per litre of milk) including variable and allocated fixed costs. Compare with the price: if cost per unit is above the long-term price, the enterprise is unprofitable unless costs fall or yields rise.

Trend analysis

Track key figures over five or more years to separate weather effects from management trends. Graphs of yield, cost per unit, gross margin and debt ratio are powerful management tools.

Diagnosing problems: example

Net farm income fell by 25%. Analysis shows: maize gross margin dropped because yields fell (physical records show below-average rain); beef gross margin held steady; fixed costs rose 15% due to new machinery depreciation and interest. Management information: the crop drop is weather-related, but the fixed cost rise is structural. Action: review machinery investment, consider contracting, and plan drought risk management.

Reporting to management

Prepare short, clear reports: key ratios with comparisons, enterprise gross margins, cost per unit, cash flow position, and a few recommendations. Use the same format each month or quarter so trends stand out. Banks and investors also expect well-prepared financial information.

Key points

  • The income statement shows profit over a period; the balance sheet shows position on a date; the cash flow statement shows cash movement.
  • Liquidity, solvency and profitability ratios need comparisons to be meaningful.
  • Physical records explain financial results.
  • Calculate enterprise gross margins and cost per unit.
  • Use trends and clear reports to drive decisions.
